text.p: Cameroon's 1996/97 cocoa crop totalled 125,800 tonnes by July 21, a few days before the season ended on August 1, against 134,000 tonnes in 1995/96, the government daily newspaper said, quoting a minister.
The Cameroon Tribune quoted commerce and industry minister Justin Ndioro as saying 100,200 tonnes had been exported with the rest sent for local processing.
Ndioro said the negative effects on bean quality from donor-sponsored liberalisation of marketing in the early 1990s had been "mitigated".

The National Cocoa and Coffee Board relaxed its export monitoring role in 1991 and stopped providing guarantees for low-interest bank credits for exporters. Much of Cameroon's cocoa is now sold on a spot basis.

Cameroon origin cocoa was discounted on world markets after the move, which the government has since blamed for a loss of bean quality due to a boom in the number of inexperienced buyers and exporters.
"Seven years after this measure which came about as part of a general globalisation of economies, the result is mitigated," Ndioro was quoted as saying.
Of 409 exporters only 53 had been actively exporting, he added.
Cameroon in July named three quality control firms to monitor 1997/98 exports.
Quality had also been hit by the inadequacy of quality controls and difficulties in supplying pesticides and insecticides, Ndioro added.
The government aimed to reduce marketing costs and put in place a system of price-setting for producers which would be in line with world levels.

For 1997/98, Ndioro said, farm cooperatives and producers would benefit from European Union STABEX funds totalling four billion CFA francs and a credit line opened with the African AFREXIMBANK commercial bank.
One European Union analyst said earlier this year that good quality cocoa plunged from 76 percent of Cammeroon's exports in 1988/89 to 17 percent in 1995/96.
